blocks.text: 1. Euclidean Distance

blocks.alt: Vector A and vector B have a straight-line distance between them

blocks.text: Euclidean distance measures straight line distance directly, giving the third of the three main candidates its own full treatment.
It computes the literal straight line distance between two points in vector space, the most geometrically intuitive of the three metrics.
2. From Similarity To Distance
As covered in Similarity Metrics, cosine similarity and dot product measure how alike two vectors are, while Euclidean distance instead measures how far apart they sit.
A smaller distance means a closer, more similar match.
3. The Pythagorean Connection

blocks.alt: Coordinate differences are squared and summed, then square rooted

blocks.text: Euclidean distance extends the familiar Pythagorean theorem into many dimensions at once.
It squares each dimension's difference, sums them, and takes the square root.
4. Bounded Below But Not Above

blocks.alt: Zero means identical while there is no maximum bound

blocks.text: As with the unbounded score range covered in Dot Product, Euclidean distance starts at zero for identical vectors.
No fixed upper limit exists, since two points can sit arbitrarily far apart.

blocks.text: 5. Sensitivity To Magnitude

blocks.alt: A longer vector gives a larger distance, even in a similar direction

blocks.text: As with keeping magnitude in play covered in Dot Product, two vectors pointing the same direction but different lengths still score as distant here.
Euclidean distance cares about the actual position in space, not just direction.

blocks.title: warn
blocks.content: Two chunks about the exact same topic, one short and one long, can receive a large Euclidean distance simply because their embeddings sit at different positions in space, even though their meaning is very similar.

blocks.text: 6. Why Text Embeddings Often Avoid It

blocks.alt: Text embeddings prefer cosine similarity over Euclidean

blocks.text: As with why text embeddings favor cosine, covered in Cosine Similarity, longer chunks with larger magnitude embeddings get penalized under Euclidean distance.
That sensitivity is often undesirable for comparing text of varying length.
7. When Euclidean Makes Sense

blocks.alt: Spatial or coordinate data works well with Euclidean

blocks.text: Image embeddings and other spatial or coordinate style data often use Euclidean distance naturally.
Position in space already carries direct, meaningful signal in those domains.

blocks.title: info
blocks.content: Physical coordinate data has actual spatial distance as its natural measure of similarity, unlike text embeddings, where direction, not raw position, tends to carry the meaningful signal.

blocks.text: 8. Relationship To Cosine On Normalized Vectors
As with normalized versus unnormalized vectors covered in Similarity Metrics, on normalized vectors, Euclidean distance and cosine similarity produce equivalent rankings.
The choice between them becomes mostly a matter of convention once vectors are normalized.

blocks.text: 9. Recognizing When Euclidean Distance Is The Right Metric

blocks.alt: Spatial or image-like embeddings point toward using Euclidean distance

blocks.text: Spatial, coordinate style, or image embeddings suit Euclidean distance well.
Comparing text chunks of varying length, on the other hand, favors cosine similarity, as covered in Cosine Similarity.
10. Worked Example
The example below demonstrates that Euclidean distance penalizes vectors of different magnitude even when they share the same direction.

code.content:
import math

def euclidean_distance(v1, v2):
    # the Pythagorean theorem extended to many dimensions
    return math.sqrt(sum((a - b) ** 2 for a, b in zip(v1, v2)))

query_embedding = [1, 2, 3]
short_chunk = [1.1, 2.1, 2.9]  # very close in position
long_chunk = [5, 10, 15]  # same direction as query, but much farther in position

dist_short = euclidean_distance(query_embedding, short_chunk)
dist_long = euclidean_distance(query_embedding, long_chunk)

print("Euclidean distance to a short, nearby chunk:")
print(f"  distance: {dist_short:.3f}")

print("\nEuclidean distance to a long chunk in the same direction:")
print(f"  distance: {dist_long:.3f}")

print("\nNotice the long chunk scores as far away despite sharing direction with the query.")

blocks.title: info
blocks.content: Running this example shows the long chunk producing a much larger Euclidean distance than the short chunk, even though both share a similar direction to the query.

blocks.text: 11. Common Mistakes

items: Using Euclidean distance to compare text chunks of very different lengths without normalizing first.
Sorting results in the wrong direction, forgetting that a smaller distance means a closer match.
Assuming Euclidean distance and cosine similarity always agree on unnormalized vectors.
Ignoring that Euclidean distance has no fixed upper bound, unlike cosine similarity's fixed range.

blocks.text: 12. Key Takeaways

items: Euclidean distance computes the literal straight line distance between two points in vector space.
Unlike cosine similarity and dot product, it measures apartness rather than alikeness.
It extends the Pythagorean theorem into many dimensions at once.
It starts at zero for identical vectors but has no fixed upper limit.
It cares about actual position in space, making it sensitive to vector magnitude.
Longer text chunks with larger magnitude embeddings can get unfairly penalized under this metric.
Spatial or coordinate style data, like image embeddings, often use Euclidean distance naturally.
On normalized vectors, Euclidean distance and cosine similarity produce equivalent rankings.
